title: Curious people: how discoveries begin with a question

summary.text: A yellow haldi stain on a white shirt can turn red in the wash. Many people have seen it happen, but few ask why. A scientist is a person who notices something, asks a question about it, and tries things to find out. In this unit you test which kitchen liquids turn haldi red. You also meet curious people from India and the world, like Tu Youyou, who found a medicine in a very old book and then tested it.
summary.art: A white school shirt on a washing stone with a bright red spot where a yellow haldi stain was, a bar of soap beside it, and a girl peering at the spot with a puzzled face.

intro.hook: Here is an old cloth with a yellow haldi stain. When a stain like this is washed, it can turn red. What do you think turns it red?
intro.text: Many grown-ups have seen a haldi stain turn red in the wash, but most never ask why. Asking why, and then trying things to find out, is what scientists do. In this unit you become a scientist in your own kitchen. You also hear true stories of curious people who found out new things.
intro.art: A child holding up an old white cloth with a yellow haldi stain, looking at it closely, with a bucket and a bar of soap nearby.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a scientist does: notices something, asks a question, and tries things to find out.
By the end I can say that anyone who is curious can be a scientist, girls and boys, from any place.
By the end I can find out which kitchen liquids turn haldi red, by testing one at a time.
By the end I can tell the story of Tu Youyou, who found a medicine for malaria.
By the end I can name a discovery from India and one from another country.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Being curious means wanting to know more about something. A curious person asks lots of questions.
terms.example: Meenakshi was curious about why the haldi stain went red, so she asked Paati.
terms.art: A girl crouching to look closely at a red spot on a shirt, with a big question mark floating above her head.

terms.meaning: A scientist is a person who finds out how the world works. They look closely, ask questions and test their ideas.
terms.example: Tu Youyou was a scientist in China. She found a new medicine for malaria.
terms.art: Four different people side by side: a woman with a notebook, a girl with a hand lens, an old man looking at the sky, and a woman holding a leaf.

terms.meaning: A discovery is finding out something about the world that people did not know before.
terms.example: Finding out that soap turns haldi red was a discovery for you.
terms.art: A child holding up a paper with a red soap spot on yellow haldi, smiling and showing it to her grandmother.

terms.meaning: A test is a way to find out if your guess is right. You try it and see what happens.
terms.example: You guessed lemon would turn haldi red. You tested it, and it stayed yellow.
terms.art: A row of small steel cups, each with a different liquid, and a yellow haldi paper with some spots red and some still yellow.

explanations.context: This card says what scientists do. It comes after the haldi test, where you did the same.
explanations.description: Scientists notice things. Then they ask a question, like 'Why did the haldi go red?' They make a guess. Then they try things to see if the guess is right. Last, they tell other people what they found, so others can try it too. There is no single fixed order. Sometimes a scientist tries things first and asks questions later. Scientists still argue about whether there is one right way to do science.
examples: You noticed haldi went red with soap. You asked which liquids do it. You tested each one.
C. V. Raman, a scientist from India, saw the deep blue sea from a ship in 1921. He asked why the sea is so blue. He spent years finding out.
Babies are curious too. When a toy does something surprising, babies pick it up and test it again.
explanations.art: Four simple pictures in a circle: an eye (notice), a question mark (ask), a hand holding a cup (try), and a mouth speaking (tell).

explanations.concept: Anyone curious can be a scientist
explanations.context: This card says who can be a scientist. The answer is: anyone who keeps asking and trying.
explanations.definition: A scientist is anyone who finds out about the world by looking closely, asking questions and testing ideas.
explanations.description: Scientists are not a special kind of person born clever. They are people who stay curious and keep trying. Some started as children. Mary Anning was about 12 when she and her brother found the bones of a huge sea animal that lived long ago, on a beach in England. Some had little money and no big laboratory. Tu Youyou never had a doctorate, the top university degree, but she found a medicine that has saved millions of lives. Women and girls have always done science, even when people tried to stop them.
examples: Mary Anning dug up fossils on the beach as a girl, in about 1811 and 1812.
Janaki Ammal, from Thalassery in Kerala, grew new kinds of sugarcane that grow well in Indian fields.
Tu Youyou, from China, found a malaria medicine by reading old books and testing.
explanations.art: A girl on a pebbly beach brushing sand from a long fossil skeleton, with cliffs behind her and a small dog at her side.

explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the haldi test, after you tried every liquid.
explanations.definition: Haldi has a yellow colouring in it. Soap and cooking soda change this colouring to red. Lemon juice changes it back to yellow.
explanations.description: The yellow in haldi comes from a colouring called curcumin. Curcumin is yellow in plain water, salt water, sugar water and lemon juice. Soap and cooking soda change it, so it looks red. Add lemon juice, and it turns yellow again. Scientists call soapy things like these bases, and sour things like lemon acids. You will learn more about them when you are older. Some mild liquid hand washes do not turn haldi red. That is a real result too.
examples: A haldi stain on a white shirt turns red when you rub soap on it.
A drop of soap water on haldi paper makes a red spot.
A drop of lemon juice on the red spot turns it yellow again.
explanations.art: Three squares of yellow haldi paper: one with a red spot labelled 'soap', one still yellow labelled 'lemon', and one where a red spot is turning back to yellow.

explanations.context: This card is about where discoveries come from: India, China, England and all over the world.
explanations.definition: A discovery is finding out something about the world that people did not know before. People in every part of the world have made them.
explanations.description: People in every land have asked questions and found answers. Aryabhata, in India about 1,500 years ago, wrote that the Earth spins round. Tu Youyou, in China, found a medicine for malaria in 1971. C. V. Raman, in Kolkata, found something new about light in 1928. Each discovery is shared, so people everywhere can use it and test it again. A discovery made in one country helps people in every country.
examples: Malaria medicine found in China is now used in India and many other countries.
Aryabhata, in India, wrote that the Earth spins, in the year 499.
Ronald Ross, working in Secunderabad, near Hyderabad, found in 1897 that mosquitoes carry malaria.
explanations.art: A round world with small pictures on it: a woman with old books in China, a man on a ship near India, an old astronomer in India looking at stars, and a girl on a beach in England.

agreed.text: Anyone who is curious and tests their ideas can find out new things.
agreed.evidence: Mary Anning found famous fossils as a girl. Tu Youyou found a medicine without a doctorate. Children find things out at home every day by trying them.

agreed.text: Soap and cooking soda turn haldi red, and lemon juice turns it yellow again.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test this at home with haldi, soap, cooking soda and lemon. It works the same way in every kitchen.

agreed.text: A guess becomes knowledge only after it is tested.
agreed.evidence: Tu Youyou guessed that heat was spoiling the medicine. She made it without much heat, and it worked. Her test showed her guess was right.

challenging.claim: Scientists are special people who are born clever.
challenging.who: A common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Famous scientists did amazing things, so it seems they must be very different from us.
challenging.against: Scientists learn by asking, trying and making mistakes, like everyone. Mary Anning started as a girl collecting shells and fossils on the beach. Many scientists say they kept going because they were curious, not because they were born knowing.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that only special people can be scientists.

challenging.claim: Old medicine books always have the right answer.
challenging.for: Tu Youyou found the clue to her malaria medicine in a book about 1,600 years old.
challenging.against: Tu Youyou's team tested hundreds of old recipes against malaria. Most did not work. Only careful testing showed which one did. An old book can give a clue, and a test shows if the clue is right.
challenging.context: This card is about old books and new tests.

challenging.claim: New ideas that sound strange must be wrong.
challenging.for: Many strange ideas do turn out to be wrong when people test them.
challenging.against: Some strange ideas turned out to be right. Many people laughed at the idea that stones fall from the sky. Then scientists studied stones that many people saw fall, and agreed. A strange idea must be tested, not laughed at or believed straight away.
challenging.context: This card is about strange new ideas, and why we test them.

big_questions.q: Many people saw haldi stains turn red and never asked why. What else might you see every day without asking about it?
big_questions.hint: Think about things in your kitchen, your bathroom and outside your window.

big_questions.q: Is a discovery still a discovery if someone else already knew it?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you felt when the haldi went red, even though Paati had seen it before.

big_questions.q: Where do questions come from? Can you make yourself curious?
big_questions.hint: Think about a time a question just popped into your head.

big_questions.q: Will people ever run out of things to discover?
big_questions.hint: Think about how each answer you found gave you a new question.

story.title: The Red Spot on Arjun's Shirt
story.note: Meenakshi, Arjun and Paati are made up. Haldi really does turn red with washing soap, and yellow again with lemon.
text: It was a Sunday morning in Madurai. Meenakshi was six. Her big brother Arjun was nine. They lived with Amma, Appa and Paati in a flat on the second floor.
At lunch, Arjun ate sambar and rice very fast. A big drop of sambar fell on his white school shirt. It left a bright yellow spot.
"Oh no," said Arjun. "That's my school shirt."
"Haldi," said Paati. "The sambar has haldi in it. Haldi is very yellow, and it sticks."
After lunch, Paati took the shirt to the bathroom. Meenakshi went with her. Paati wet the shirt and rubbed the yellow spot with a bar of washing soap.
Meenakshi stared. "Paati! The spot is going red!"
It was true. Where the soap touched the yellow, it turned red, like kumkum.
"Yes," said Paati. "Haldi always does that with soap. I have seen it since I was a little girl."
"But why?" asked Meenakshi.
Paati stopped rubbing. She thought for a moment. "Do you know, I never asked," she said. "I have washed a hundred haldi stains. I always saw it go red. But I never asked why."
"Can we find out?" asked Meenakshi.
Paati smiled. "Let's try. First, what do you think makes it red?"
Meenakshi thought. "Maybe it's the water," she said. "Or maybe it's the rubbing."
"Good guesses," said Paati. "How can we check?"
They went to the kitchen. Paati mixed a little haldi with water in a small steel katori. It was bright yellow. She painted some of it on an old white paper with her finger.
Meenakshi dipped her finger in plain water. She touched the yellow paper. The spot stayed yellow. "Not the water," she said.
She rubbed the paper hard with a dry finger. It stayed yellow. "Not the rubbing."
Then she wet her finger and rubbed it on the bar of soap. She touched the paper. A red spot came up at once.
"It's the soap!" she shouted.
Arjun came into the kitchen. "What are you two doing?"
"Finding out why your shirt went red," said Meenakshi. "It's the soap. Watch." She made another red spot.
"What else can turn it red?" asked Arjun.
"Let's find out," said Meenakshi. Now she was the teacher.
They tried salt water. It stayed yellow. They tried sugar water. Yellow. They tried lemon juice. Yellow.
Then Paati took the tin of cooking soda that Amma used for the idli batter on busy days. She mixed a pinch with water. Meenakshi dabbed it on the paper. The spot turned orange-red.
"Soap and cooking soda," said Meenakshi slowly. "Those two make it red. The others don't."
Arjun looked at the red spots. "Can you make it yellow again?"
Meenakshi did not know. She tried lemon juice on a red spot. Slowly, the red went pale. Then it was yellow again.
"It came back!" said Arjun.
That evening, Appa came home. Meenakshi showed him the paper. She showed him the red spots and the yellow spots, and told him what each one was.
"Who taught you this?" asked Appa.
"Nobody," said Meenakshi. "I asked a question. Then we tried things."
Paati laughed. "Meenakshi taught me," she said. "Sixty years of washing, and today I found out something new."
Appa smiled. "You know who does that? Scientists. They ask a question, and then they try things to find out."
Meenakshi looked at her yellow and red paper. "Then I'm a scientist," she said.
"And so is Paati," said Arjun.
That night, Meenakshi lay in bed and looked at the ceiling fan. Why does it make a whirring sound? she wondered. She smiled in the dark. Tomorrow she would find out.
story.epiphany: Meenakshi sees the haldi stain turn red and asks why. By trying one thing at a time, she finds that soap and cooking soda turn haldi red. She realises that asking and trying is what scientists do, and that her grandmother, who saw it for sixty years, is finding out with her.
ask: What did Meenakshi notice about Arjun's shirt?
How did Meenakshi find out it was the soap, and not the water or the rubbing?
Paati had seen haldi go red for sixty years. Why did she only find out what did it that day?
art: A grandmother in a cotton saree rubbing a bar of soap on a white shirt in a bathroom, with a red spot appearing, and a girl staring at it.
A girl and her grandmother at a kitchen counter with small steel katoris, dabbing liquids on yellow paper.
A girl showing a yellow paper with red spots to her father, who has just come home, with her brother and grandmother smiling beside her.

games.title: True or False? Who Found Out
games.context: This is a card game of surprising facts. Some are true and some are false. People found out each one by asking and testing. You jump to the True side or the False side, then turn the card over.

items.f: The Earth is round, like a ball.
items.b: True. People in ancient Greece and India worked this out long ago. Today, photos from space show it.

items.f: The Sun goes round the Earth.
items.b: False. The Earth goes round the Sun. Aryabhata in India also wrote that the Earth spins.
True. The Sun is our closest star. The other stars are suns very far away.

items.f: The Moon makes its own light.
items.b: False. The Moon shines because sunlight falls on it.
True. Clouds are made of tiny drops of water, or tiny bits of ice.
False. Air is very light, but it does weigh something.
True. An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
True. A touch-me-not plant folds up their leaves when you touch them.

items.f: The Earth spins round once every day.
items.b: True. One spin makes one day and one night.

items.f: The Himalayas are still growing taller.
items.b: True. They grow a tiny bit each year, too slowly to see.
False. Birds are dinosaurs. The crow at your window is one.
True. You can test this one yourself.

rules: Put the TRUE sign on one side of the room and the FALSE sign on the other.
Stand in the middle. The grown-up reads a card aloud.
Jump to TRUE or FALSE. Say why you think so.
The grown-up turns the card over and reads the back.
If you were right, keep the card. If not, put it in the middle.
When the cards are finished, count your cards.

setup.art: A room with a TRUE sign with a tick on one wall and a FALSE sign with a cross on the other, and a child standing in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Put the two signs on opposite sides.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card aloud while a child jumps towards the TRUE sign.
setup.caption: 2. Listen, then jump to True or False. Say why.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Put the two signs on opposite walls.
flow.say: Each card tells a fact. Some are true and some are false. You jump to the side you think is right.
flow.kid: Some cards are true. Some are false. Jump to your answer.

flow.do: Read each card aloud. Wait for the jump and a reason. Then read the back.
flow.say: Here is a card. Is it true or false? Why do you think so? Now let's turn it over.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Jump to True or False. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the Moon makes its own light, or does not?
good: It is bright, so it makes light.
The Sun shines on it.

flow.parent: Wrong jumps are good. Many grown-ups think the Moon makes its own light, and that all dinosaurs are gone. Ask how people might have found out.

flow.do: Pick one surprising card together. Talk about how someone found it out.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? How do you think someone found that out?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you? How did someone find out?

check.q: How did people find out that soap turns haldi red?
check.why: People found out by trying it. You can try it too, and see the same thing. That is how a test works.

games.title: Notice, Wonder, Try: a board game
games.context: This is a board game about being curious. Each square asks you to notice something, wonder about something, or try something small. The first to reach the end wins.

printables.title: A path of 15 squares to draw
items: Notice: say one thing you see in this room that is red.
Wonder: ask one question about the window.
Try: drop a spoon and a paper ball together. Which lands first?
Notice: listen. Say one sound you can hear.
Wonder: ask one question about your hands.
Try: blow on your hand softly, then hard. What changes?
Notice: say one thing that smells good in the kitchen.
Wonder: ask one question about the sky.
Try: hold a steel spoon and a wooden spoon. Which feels colder?
Story: name one curious person from this unit.
Notice: find something that is round.
Wonder: ask one question about an animal you know.
Try: put a drop of water on a steel plate and on a cloth. What happens to each?

printables.title: 4 counters and a dice
items: a dice, or six folded paper slips numbered 1 to 3, twice

rules: Take turns to roll the dice and move.
Do what your square says. Everyone listens.
If you do it, stay there. If you are stuck, the others can help.
The first player to reach Finish wins.

setup.art: A winding path of 15 squares drawn on a big sheet, with small drawings of an eye, a question mark and a hand on the squares.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the path of squares.

setup.art: Two children and a grandmother around the board, one child dropping a spoon and a paper ball at the same time.
setup.caption: 2. Move, then do what your square says.

flow.do: Draw the path together. Read each square aloud.
flow.say: Some squares ask you to notice, some to wonder, some to try. Let's draw the path.
flow.kid: Help draw the path. Notice, wonder, try!

flow.do: Play the game. Help with the Try squares.
flow.say: Roll and move. What does your square say? Let's do it.
flow.kid: Roll and move. Do what your square says.
flow.parent: Wonder squares have no right answer. Any real question counts. If a Try square gives a surprise, stop and ask why.

flow.do: After the game, ask the last question.
flow.say: Which square was the most fun? Did any Try square surprise you?
flow.kid: Which square was most fun? Did anything surprise you?

options: Why do birds sit on wires?
check.why: A wonder is a question. 'Why do birds sit on wires?' is a question. The others say what happened or what you see.

experiments.title: The Haldi Test: which kitchen liquids turn haldi red?
experiments.context: In this experiment you paint yellow haldi on paper. Then you touch it with six kitchen liquids, one at a time. You find out which ones turn the haldi red.
experiments.question: A haldi stain can turn red in the wash. Which kitchen liquids turn haldi red?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will plain water, lemon juice, salt water, sugar water, soap water and cooking soda water turn the haldi red? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same haldi paper for every liquid. We put one drop of each liquid in its own box. We use a clean cotton bud or a clean spoon tip each time. Only the liquid changes.
results_table: What I saw: red or yellow?

materials.item: haldi (turmeric powder)
a sheet of white paper, such as an old notebook page
6 small steel katoris or cups
a lemon, cut by a grown-up
salt and sugar
a bar of washing soap or bathing soap, or a pinch of washing powder
cooking soda (meetha soda, used for idli or pakoda)
cotton buds, or a spoon wiped clean each time
old newspaper to work on

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the lemon and mixes the soap and cooking soda water. Keep soap water and lemon away from eyes. Haldi stains clothes and fingers yellow, so wear old clothes and work on newspaper.

schedule.what: Guess, make the haldi paper, test six liquids, and say what you found.

experiments.record: The haldi paper itself, with each box named, and the results table with a guess and a result for each liquid.

setup.art: Six small steel katoris in a row on newspaper, each with a drawn label: a water drop, a lemon, salt, sugar, a soap bar and a soda tin.
setup.caption: 1. Set out six liquids, each in its own katori.

setup.art: A child painting yellow haldi water onto white paper with her fingers, with six boxes drawn in pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Paint the paper yellow with haldi. Draw six boxes.

setup.art: A child dabbing a cotton bud from one katori into one box on the yellow paper, and that box turning red.
setup.caption: 3. Dab one liquid in each box. Watch the colour.

setup.art: The haldi paper with two red boxes and four yellow boxes, next to a results table with ticks.
setup.caption: 4. Mark what you saw. Which boxes went red?

flow.do: 1. Show the yellow haldi and the six liquids. 2. Draw the results table together. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for each liquid. Write the guesses.
flow.say: A haldi stain can turn red in the wash. Which of our kitchen liquids does that? For each one, red or yellow? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the six liquids. Which ones will turn haldi red? Why?

ask.q: Which ones do you think will turn it red? Why?
good: Lemon, because it is strong.
Not water, because water just makes it wet.
Salt, because it is like soap.

flow.parent: Don't say what will happen. Many children guess lemon will turn it red, because lemon is strong and sour. Write every guess down.

flow.do: 1. Put a little of each liquid in its own katori. Plain water. Lemon juice. Salt water. Sugar water. 2. Rub the wet soap bar in a katori of water until it is cloudy. 3. Stir a pinch of cooking soda into water.
flow.say: I am making soap water and soda water. You can help with salt and sugar. Stir until they disappear.
flow.kid: Help stir the salt and the sugar into water.
flow.parent: Use a bar of washing soap or bathing soap, or washing powder. Some mild liquid hand washes and shampoos do not turn haldi red. Keep soap water away from eyes.

flow.do: 1. Mix half a teaspoon of haldi with three spoons of water. 2. Paint it thickly on the paper with fingers or a brush. 3. Draw six boxes in pencil and write or draw a liquid in each.
flow.say: Paint the whole paper yellow. Make it nice and thick. Now we draw six boxes, one for each liquid.
flow.kid: Paint the paper yellow with haldi. Draw six boxes.
flow.parent: The paper can stay damp. The colour change shows even better on damp haldi.

flow.do: 1. Dip a clean cotton bud in plain water. 2. Dab it in the first box. 3. Wait and watch for ten seconds. 4. Mark the table. 5. Do the same for each liquid, with a clean bud each time.
flow.say: One drop, in its own box. Watch it. Is it red or yellow? Now the next one, with a clean bud.
flow.kid: Dab one liquid in its box. Watch. Is it red?
flow.parent: Soap water turns the haldi deep red at once. Cooking soda water usually turns it orange-red. Water, lemon, salt and sugar leave it yellow. If the soap box stays yellow, try a different soap bar or washing powder.

flow.do: Look at the paper and the table together. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: What did you find out? Which liquids turned haldi red? How do you know? Was any guess different from what happened?
flow.kid: Which liquids turned it red? How do you know?

good: Soap and cooking soda.
The soap one went the reddest.

check.q: Your soap box went red. Your lemon box stayed yellow. What did the test show?
options: Soap turns haldi red, and lemon does not
check.why: Each liquid had its own box, and only the liquid changed. So the red came from the soap, not from the paper or the water.

experiments.title: Back to Yellow: can the red spot change back?
experiments.context: In this experiment you take a red spot from the haldi test. You find out if anything can turn it yellow again.
experiments.question: Once soap has turned haldi red, can we turn it yellow again?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the red spot stay red for ever? Could lemon, water or salt water change it back? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We put one drop of a different liquid on each red spot. All the red spots were made with the same soap water. Only the liquid we add changes.
results_table: Liquid added to the red spot

materials.item: the haldi paper from the haldi test, or a new one
soap water, lemon juice, plain water and salt water, from the haldi test
cotton buds

experiments.safety: Keep lemon juice and soap water away from eyes.

schedule.what: Make three red spots with soap. Add water, salt water and lemon. Watch which spot turns yellow.

experiments.record: Draw three red spots and colour each one the way it looked after you added a liquid.

setup.art: A yellow haldi paper with three red soap spots in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Make three red spots with soap water.

setup.art: A child adding a drop of lemon juice to one red spot, and the spot turning yellow again.
setup.caption: 2. Add a different liquid to each spot. Watch.

flow.do: Make three red spots on the haldi paper with soap water.
flow.say: Here are three red spots. Can we make one yellow again? What might do it? Why?
flow.kid: Can a red spot go yellow again? What could do it?

good: Water could wash it away.
Lemon, because lemon kept it yellow before.

flow.do: Add a few drops of plain water to spot one, salt water to spot two and lemon juice to spot three. Watch for half a minute.
flow.say: Water on the first. Salt water on the second. Lemon on the third. Watch closely.
flow.kid: Add one liquid to each red spot. Watch.
flow.parent: The lemon spot fades to orange and then yellow. It may need a few more drops. Water and salt water leave the spot red.

flow.do: Add soap water to the yellow lemon spot again. Talk about what you saw.
flow.say: Now soap on the lemon spot. What happens? What does that tell us?
flow.kid: Put soap on it again. What happens?

check.q: Soap made haldi red. Lemon made it yellow again. What happens if you add soap again?
check.why: The haldi colouring is still there. Soap turns it red, and lemon turns it yellow, as many times as you like.

activities.title: I Notice, I Wonder: at the window
activities.context: In this activity you look out of a window for a few minutes. You say what you notice, and then what you wonder. Scientists start like this.

materials.item: a window or a balcony
paper and crayons

schedule.what: Look out of a window. Say three things you notice and three things you wonder.

activities.record: A drawing of one thing you noticed, with your wonder question written by a grown-up underneath.

setup.art: A girl and her grandmother looking out of a flat window at a tree, a crow on a wire and clouds.
setup.caption: 1. Look out quietly. What do you notice?

setup.art: A child's drawing of a crow on a wire, with a question written below it: 'Why do crows sit on wires?'
setup.caption: 2. Draw one thing. Say your wonder question.

flow.do: Look out of the window together, quietly, for two minutes. Then take turns to say 'I notice…'
flow.say: Let's look quietly for two minutes. Then tell me three things you notice. Start with 'I notice'.
flow.kid: Look out quietly. Then say, 'I notice…' three times.

good: I notice a crow on the wire.
I notice the clouds are moving.
I notice a man selling vegetables.

flow.do: Now take turns to say 'I wonder…' about the things you noticed.
flow.say: Now let's wonder. Start with 'I wonder why' or 'I wonder how'.
flow.kid: Now say, 'I wonder…' three times.

good: I wonder why crows sit on wires.
I wonder where the clouds go.

flow.parent: Every real question is a good one. Don't answer them now. Write them down, so you can find out together later.

flow.do: Your child draws one thing they noticed. Write their wonder question underneath.
flow.say: Draw one thing you noticed. I'll write your question under it.
flow.kid: Draw one thing. Tell me your question.

activities.title: The Secret Red Message
activities.context: In this activity you write a secret message in soap water on white paper. It dries and disappears. Then you brush haldi water over it, and your message comes back in red.

materials.item: a sheet of white paper
soap water, made by rubbing a wet bar of washing soap in a little water
a cotton bud or a thin paintbrush
haldi mixed with water
materials.qty: half a teaspoon of haldi in three spoons of water

materials.item: a wide brush, or a cotton ball

activities.safety: Keep soap water away from eyes. Haldi stains clothes, so work on newspaper.

schedule.what: Write a message in soap water. Let it dry. Brush haldi water over it, and watch the message appear.

activities.record: The secret message paper, with the red writing on yellow.

setup.art: A child writing with a cotton bud dipped in soap water on white paper, and the writing almost invisible.
setup.caption: 1. Write in soap water. Let it dry.

setup.art: A grown-up brushing yellow haldi water over the paper, and red letters appearing.
setup.caption: 2. Brush haldi water over it. Watch the message appear.

flow.do: 1. Make the soap water. 2. Your child dips a cotton bud and writes a word or draws a shape on the white paper. 3. Let it dry under the fan for about five minutes.
flow.say: Write a word or draw a star with soap water. Press hard. Can you still see it when it dries?
flow.kid: Write or draw with soap water. Let it dry.
flow.parent: Thick soap water works best. Go over the letters twice.

flow.do: Ask for a guess before you brush.
flow.say: When I brush yellow haldi over the paper, what will happen to your hidden word? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: What will happen when we brush on haldi? Why?

good: The word will go red, because soap turns haldi red.
It will all go yellow.

flow.do: Brush haldi water gently over the whole paper.
flow.say: Watch. What do you see? Why did the word come back?
flow.kid: Watch the paper. What do you see? Why?

check.q: Why did the hidden word turn red?
options: The soap was still on the paper, and soap turns haldi red
check.why: The soap dried and became hard to see, but it was still there. Where the haldi touched soap, it turned red.

activities.title: Be Tu Youyou: the clue in the old book
activities.context: In this activity you act out the true story of Tu Youyou. She read very old books to find a medicine for malaria, then tested what she found. You hunt for clue cards hidden in your home.

materials.item: 4 small papers for clue cards, written by a grown-up
an old book or notebook to be the old medicine book
a green leaf, from a potted plant or a bunch of coriander, to be the plant
a cup of water, for pretend

schedule.what: Hear the story. Hunt for four clue cards. Act out the test.

activities.record: Tell the story back to a family member, using the four clue cards.

setup.art: A child opening an old notebook and finding a small folded clue card inside.
setup.caption: 1. Find the clue cards hidden around the home.

setup.art: A child pretending to be a scientist, holding a green leaf and a cup of cool water, with a grown-up watching.
setup.caption: 2. Act out Tu Youyou's test.

flow.do: Before you start, write and hide four clue cards. Put card 1 in an old book. It says: Soak the plant in cold water. Card 2 says: Try again and again. Card 3 says: Heat can spoil a medicine. Card 4 says: Test carefully, to be safe. Then tell the short story.
flow.say: Long ago, many people were ill with malaria, an illness spread by mosquito bites. A scientist called Tu Youyou looked for a medicine in very old books. Let's hunt for her clues.
flow.kid: Tu Youyou looked for a medicine in old books. Find her clues!

flow.do: Your child hunts for the cards. Read each one aloud when it is found.
flow.say: You found a clue! Let me read it. What do you think it means?
flow.kid: Find a clue. What does it say?
flow.parent: This is a game. The leaf and water are pretend. Never make or drink a medicine from a plant at home.

flow.do: Act out the story. Your child is Tu Youyou. You are her team.
flow.say: Tu Youyou read that the plant was soaked in cold water. But people usually boiled plants to make medicine. What did she wonder?
flow.kid: You are Tu Youyou. You read 'cold water'. What do you wonder?

good: Maybe heat spoils the medicine.
Why cold water and not hot?

check.q: Tu Youyou guessed that heat was spoiling the medicine. What did she do next?
options: She made it without much heat and tested it
check.why: A guess has to be tested. She made the medicine without much heat, and it worked. The test showed her guess was right.

projects.title: My Wonder Book: three days
projects.context: In this project you make a small book of your own questions. Day 1 you write wonders. Day 2 you test one. Day 3 you tell someone what you found.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with thread
crayons or colour pencils

schedule.what: Make the book. A grown-up writes down three of your wonder questions. Draw a picture for each.
Choose one question you can test at home. Guess, try it, and draw what happened.
Read your Wonder Book to someone in the family. Tell them what you found.

projects.record: The finished Wonder Book, read aloud to a family member.

setup.art: A small handmade book with 'My Wonder Book' on the cover and a big question mark.
setup.caption: 1. Make a little book.

setup.art: An open page with a child's drawing of a spoon and a paper ball falling, and a question above it.
setup.caption: 2. Test one question. Draw what happened.

flow.do: 1. Fold and staple the book. 2. Ask for three 'I wonder' questions. 3. Write each on a page. Your child draws a picture.
flow.say: What do you wonder about? Tell me three questions. I'll write them, and you draw.
flow.kid: Tell me three things you wonder. Draw one picture for each.

flow.do: Choose one question you can test safely at home. Ask for a guess and a reason, then try it.
flow.say: Which question can we test today? What do you guess will happen? Why? Let's try it.
flow.kid: Pick one question. Guess. Then try it.
flow.parent: Good home questions: Which sinks, a steel spoon or a plastic one? Which dries faster, a wet cloth in the sun or in the shade? Does the crow come back at the same time each day?

flow.do: Your child reads the book to someone, with your help.
flow.say: Read your book to Appa or Paati. Tell them what you found, and what you want to find out next.
flow.kid: Read your book to someone. Tell them what you found.

good: The steel spoon sank and the plastic one floated.
The cloth in the sun dried first.

challenges.title: The Hidden Festival Card
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Make a greeting card with a hidden message. The message must stay hidden until your friend makes it appear.
challenges.problem: Make a card for Pongal, Onam, Diwali, Eid, Christmas or a birthday. The message inside must be hidden, and appear only when someone brushes it with haldi water.
constraints: The message must be hard to see before it is revealed.
Your friend must be able to reveal it on their own, with your instructions.
materials: soap water and a cotton bud
haldi water and a brush or cotton ball
crayons for the outside of the card
general: Write the message in soap water and let it dry.
Draw a picture on the front with crayons.
creative: Write the instructions on the front: 'Brush me with haldi water!'
Draw a kolam or a rangoli pattern in soap water, so a pattern appears in red.
Send a little packet of haldi with the card.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own hidden card. Test it on a spare paper first. Did the message stay hidden until it was brushed?

setup.art: A folded white card with crayon flowers on the front and the words 'Brush me with haldi water!'
setup.caption: 1. Make a card. Write the secret part in soap water.

setup.art: A friend brushing yellow haldi water inside the card, and a red kolam pattern appearing.
setup.caption: 2. Your friend brushes it with haldi. The message appears.

flow.do: Talk about the challenge. Ask for ideas.
flow.say: How can we hide a message so only haldi can show it? What should it say?
flow.kid: How will you hide your message? What will it say?

good: Write it in soap water.
Use soap, because soap turns haldi red.

flow.do: Your child writes the message or draws a pattern in thick soap water and lets it dry. Then they decorate the outside.
flow.say: Write your message in soap water. Let it dry. Now decorate the front.
flow.kid: Write in soap water. Let it dry. Decorate the front.
flow.parent: Test a small piece first. Thin soap water may give only a faint pink.

flow.do: Test a spare paper made the same way. Talk about it.
flow.say: Did the message stay hidden? Did it appear when you brushed it? What would you change?
flow.kid: Did it stay hidden? Did it appear? What would you change?

videos.title: Tu Youyou and the malaria medicine: a short film
videos.why: Tells the true story of how Tu Youyou found artemisinin in an old book and tested it.
videos.check: Find a real, accurate film suitable for young children, for example from the Nobel Prize channel. Check it says she used a low-heat method, and that the clue came from Ge Hong's book.

videos.title: Turmeric turns red with soap: kitchen science
videos.why: Shows haldi turning red with soap and yellow again with lemon, the same as the haldi test.
videos.check: Check it uses ordinary soap or washing powder and lemon, and does not give wrong safety advice.

videos.title: Mary Anning, the girl who found sea dragons
videos.why: A true story of a girl who found famous fossils on an English beach.
videos.check: Check the dates (the ichthyosaur, 1811 to 1812) and that her brother Joseph is named.

opts: Notices, asks questions and tests ideas
quiz.why: Scientists find out by noticing, asking and testing. Anyone can do these things, with or without a white coat.

opts: Anyone who is curious and tests their ideas
quiz.why: Girls, boys, women and men from every country have made discoveries. Mary Anning started as a girl.

quiz.p: In the haldi test, which liquid turned the haldi red?
quiz.why: Soap turns haldi red. Lemon juice and sugar water leave it yellow.

quiz.p: In the haldi test, why did each liquid get its own box?
opts: So we could tell which liquid made the colour change
To make the paper look nice
Because the paper was too big
quiz.why: If two liquids touched the same box, we would not know which one changed the colour. One liquid in each box keeps the test fair.

quiz.p: Tu Youyou found a clue for her medicine. Where?
opts: In a very old book of medicine
quiz.why: She read a book written about 1,600 years ago. It said to soak the plant in cold water.

quiz.p: Tu Youyou guessed that heat was spoiling the medicine. How did she find out if she was right?
opts: She made it without much heat and tested it
quiz.why: She tested her guess. The medicine made without much heat worked.

quiz.p: Janaki Ammal grew new kinds of sugarcane. Which country was she from?
quiz.why: Janaki Ammal was from Thalassery in Kerala, India. Tu Youyou was from China, and Mary Anning from England.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl of six in Kochi, guesses that salt turns haldi red. What should she do?
opts: Test it with salt water on haldi paper
Ask her friend to guess too
quiz.why: A guess needs a test. If Kavya tries salt water on haldi, she will see it stays yellow.

quiz.p: A red soap spot is on yellow haldi paper. You add lemon juice. What happens?
quiz.why: Lemon turns the red haldi colouring back to yellow.

quiz.p: Paati saw haldi stains go red for sixty years. Why did she only find out what did it when Meenakshi asked?
opts: Because they asked a question and tested it
quiz.why: Seeing something is the start. Asking why and testing is how you find out.

items.p: Which liquids turned haldi red in your test? Put each in a box.
items.a: Soap water and cooking soda water turned red. Lemon juice, salt water and plain water stayed yellow.
items.why: A strong answer comes from the child's own haldi paper, not from memory. If their soap box stayed yellow, they may have used a mild hand wash.

items.p: Draw your haldi paper. Colour the boxes that went red.
items.a: A yellow paper with red boxes for soap and cooking soda.
items.why: A strong drawing shows which liquid was in each box, and colours only those that changed.
items.art: An empty rectangle with six empty boxes drawn inside it.

items.p: Remember the Haldi Test? You put lemon juice on the yellow haldi. What happened?
items.why: Lemon juice leaves haldi yellow. Many children guess lemon will turn it red, because it is sour and strong.

items.p: Draw a line from each person to what they found.
pairs: fossil bones of a sea animal
items.why: Each of these people was curious, asked a question and found something out. That includes you.

items.p: Only grown-ups can make discoveries.
items.why: False. Mary Anning found famous fossils as a girl. You made a discovery in the haldi test.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: how do you know soap turns haldi red?
items.a: I put soap water on haldi paper and the spot went red. The other boxes stayed yellow.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test, what the child saw, not just 'Paati said so'.

items.p: Here is a girl being a scientist. Put an E on what she notices with, a Q on her question, and an H on what she tests with.
items.a: E on her eyes, Q on the question mark above her head, H on her hands holding the cotton bud.
items.why: Scientists notice with their senses, ask questions and test with their hands and tools.
items.art: A girl with big eyes looking at haldi paper, a question mark above her head, and her hand dabbing with a cotton bud.

items.p: Which one is NOT a question?
items.why: 'The fan is on' tells us something. The others ask something. Scientists start with questions.

items.p: Who taught Paati something new in the story?
items.why: Meenakshi asked why, and tested soap, water and rubbing. Paati learned with her. A child can teach a grown-up.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai talk about scientists.

views.says: Scientists are very clever people in big laboratories.
Anyone who asks questions and tests them is a scientist.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the haldi test or a story from this unit. Then say one thing the other friend got right.
items.a: Many children agree with Farhan, because they did the haldi test at home and found something out. Lakshmi is right that many scientists work in laboratories and learn a lot.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence, like Mary Anning on the beach or the haldi test in the kitchen. It is also fair to the other side.

items.p: Put the steps of the Haldi Test in order.
items: Guess which liquids will turn it red
Dab each liquid in its own box
a: Guess which liquids will turn it red
Dab each liquid in its own box
items.why: Scientists guess first, then test, then say what they found.

items.p: Draw the red spot after you added lemon juice in Back to Yellow.
items.a: A yellow spot, or a pale orange one turning yellow.
items.why: Lemon juice turns the red haldi colouring yellow again. A strong drawing shows the spot yellow.
items.art: An empty circle on a yellow background.

items.p: Your hidden soap word turned red when you brushed haldi on it. What does that show?
opts: The soap was still there, though you could not see it
items.why: The dried soap was hard to see, but it was still on the paper. The haldi showed where it was.

items.p: Fill the gap: A guess becomes knowledge only after we ____ it.
items.why: A guess is an idea. A test shows whether the idea is right.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: what is one question you wonder about? How could you test it?
items.a: For example: Does a wet cloth dry faster in the sun? I could hang one in the sun and one in the shade and check which dries first.
items.why: A strong answer has a real question and a test that changes only one thing.

items.p: Tu Youyou's team tested hundreds of old recipes, and most did not work against malaria.
items.why: True. Testing showed which recipe worked. An old book gave a clue, and testing showed it was right.

items.p: Meera, a girl in Hyderabad, and her grandfather talk about the old book.

views.says: Old books are always right. That's how Tu Youyou found her medicine.
Old books can be wrong. We should only trust new things.

items.ask: Who is right? Use Tu Youyou's story. What would you tell each of them?
items.a: Neither is fully right. The old book gave Tu Youyou a clue, but most old recipes did not work. She tested them to find out which one did.
items.why: A strong answer says that an old idea and a new idea both need testing. It gives each person credit for part of their view.

items.p: Here is a map of the world. Put a T where Tu Youyou worked, an R where C. V. Raman worked, and an M where Mary Anning found fossils.
items.a: T on China, R on India, M on England.
items.why: Discoveries come from every part of the world. A strong answer puts T in China, R in India and M in England.
items.art: A simple world map showing India, China and England clearly outlined, with a star for each.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does to haldi.
items.why: Soap and cooking soda turn haldi red. Lemon keeps it yellow, and turns red haldi yellow again.

items.p: Many people have seen haldi stains go red and never asked why. Say it to a grown-up: why do you think they never asked?
items.a: For example: They were busy. They saw it so often that it did not seem strange.
items.why: A strong answer sees that things we see every day stop surprising us. Scientists keep asking about ordinary things.

applications: Doctors test new medicines carefully before people use them, the way Tu Youyou did.
Cooks and grandmothers know many kitchen facts, like haldi turning red, that started as someone noticing.
Scientists share what they find, so people in other countries can test it and use it.
Asking questions and testing helps at school, at home and in every job.
Malaria medicines found by testing are used in India and many other countries.

spotted.text: A haldi stain on a shirt turning red when it is washed with soap.
spotted.art: A white shirt in a bucket with a red spot where a yellow sambar stain was.

spotted.text: Traditional kumkum, the red powder, is made by mixing haldi with chuna, the lime used with paan. The chuna turns the haldi red.
spotted.art: A small brass box of red kumkum next to a heap of yellow haldi and a little pot of white chuna.

spotted.text: Mosquito nets over beds in homes and hospitals, to stop the mosquito bites that spread malaria.
spotted.art: A bed with a white mosquito net tucked in, in a room with a ceiling fan.

spotted.text: Science centres, like the Visvesvaraya Museum in Bengaluru, full of things to touch and try.
spotted.art: Children pressing buttons and turning wheels at a science museum display.

spotted.text: A crow at the window, which scientists now call a kind of dinosaur.
spotted.art: A house crow sitting on a balcony railing, with a faint dinosaur shadow behind her.

open_questions.q: Why are some people more curious than others?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists still argue about this. Some think it is how we are born, and some think it is how we are brought up. Most think it is both.

open_questions.q: What will be the next big discovery?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody knows. A big discovery is something nobody knows yet, so nobody can say what it will be.

open_questions.q: Are other animals curious the way we are?
open_questions.why_open: Crows, octopuses, rats and many other animals explore new things. Scientists are still finding out what curiosity is like for each of them.

ask_kids: What did you notice today that you had never noticed before?
What is one thing you wonder about right now?
If you could ask a scientist one question, what would it be?
What could we test at dinner tonight?
Who in our family is the most curious? Why do you think so?

jokes.j: What is a scientist's favourite word?
Why did the curious girl bring a ladder to school?
jokes.a: She wanted to find out what was on the top shelf.

jokes.j: What did the yellow spot say to the lemon?
jokes.a: Thanks for making me myself again!

jokes.j: Why did the question mark go to the doctor?
jokes.a: Nobody had an answer for him.

jokes.j: What do you call a scientist who reads old books?
Why was the soap so good at secrets?
jokes.a: Its messages stay hidden until haldi comes along.

jokes.j: Why did the crow sit on the wire all day?
jokes.a: To find out if wires are comfy.

jokes.j: Why did Meenakshi stare at the fan all night?
jokes.a: She was a fan of finding out!

maths.problem: Meenakshi tested 6 liquids on haldi. 2 turned it red. How many stayed yellow?
maths.explain: 6 liquids in all. 2 went red. 6 take away 2 is 4.
maths.context: This is about the Haldi Test, where you put six liquids on haldi paper.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the red ones shows how many liquids left haldi yellow.

maths.problem: Lakshmi guessed that 4 liquids would turn haldi red. Only 2 did. Was her guess too many or too few? By how many?
maths.explain: 4 is more than 2. 4 take away 2 is 2. She guessed 2 more than really turned red.
maths.context: This is about the Haldi Test, where you guessed first and then tested.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the guess with the result shows how far off the guess was.

maths.problem: Arjun made a tally of the colours in his test: red, yellow, yellow, red, yellow, yellow. Make tally marks for red and for yellow. Which colour came up more?
maths.answer: Red: 2 tally marks. Yellow: 4 tally marks. Yellow came up more.
maths.explain: Count each colour and make one mark for each. Yellow has 4 marks and red has 2, so yellow came up more.
maths.context: This is about the Haldi Test, with six boxes on the haldi paper.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks help us count results quickly and see which happened more often.

founder: ideas/by_topic/how-we-know.md, 'Stories of science and the True/False card game': the founder's true-or-false fact cards. Used for game g1, rewritten for age 6, with each answer saying how people found out. 'Trees don't talk to each other' was left out because it needs more than one line to explain fairly.

ideas/by_topic/how-we-know.md, 'Grade concept grid: Fringe Science', Grade 1: new ideas must be tested, not just imagined, and some strange ideas later succeed. Used for the 'challenging' cards and for the guess-then-test thread.
ideas/by_topic/how-we-know.md, SCI Cards: Tu Youyou (cold extraction clue from Ge Hong, tested on herself first). Used for how_we_found_out and activity a3.

Ladder: Level 3 (sci.how-we-know.stories-of-discovery.L3) is about lucky accidents and missing names, with the Too-Weak Tape Test, Hot or Cold freezing, Jocelyn Bell's pulsar, the curd story, penicillin and the panakam credit game. This unit repeats none of those. It comes first: scientists are curious people who notice, ask and test, and anyone can do it. Level 3 then shows that discoveries often come from surprises and accidents, and asks who gets the credit.
science: Curcumin, the yellow colouring of turmeric, changes from yellow to red-brown as the solution becomes alkaline (above about pH 7.5 to 8.6), and returns to yellow in acid. Bar soap and washing powder are alkaline (about pH 9 to 11). Sodium bicarbonate solution is about pH 8.3 and gives an orange-red. Some mild liquid hand washes are near neutral and give little change. Turmeric paper as an indicator is a standard school activity (NCERT Class 7 Science, acids, bases and salts).

Tu Youyou: joined Project 523 in 1969 as head of a research group at the Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Beijing. Her team screened over 2,000 recipes and tested about 380 extracts. Ge Hong's 'Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies' (about 340 CE) says to soak a handful of qinghao in water, wring out the juice and drink it. She used a low-temperature ether extraction, and sample 191 was fully effective in mice and monkeys in October 1971. She and colleagues took the extract themselves before the first patient trials in 1972. Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2015 (shared with William C. Campbell and Satoshi Omura). She had no doctorate, no medical degree and no training abroad. Source: Tu Youyou, Nobel lecture, 2015, and Nobel Prize press release, 2015.
Mary Anning (1799 to 1847), Lyme Regis: her brother Joseph found the skull of an ichthyosaur in 1811, and Mary found the rest of the skeleton in 1812, aged about 12 or 13.
E. K. Janaki Ammal (1897 to 1984), born in Thalassery (Tellicherry), Kerala: worked on sugarcane hybrids at the Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore, from 1934.
C. V. Raman: voyage on the SS Narkunda in 1921, the blue colour of the sea, and the Raman effect with K. S. Krishnan, 1928. Nobel Prize in Physics, 1930.
Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya (499 CE): the Earth rotates on its axis (Gola section, verse 9, the boat simile).
Ronald Ross found malaria parasites in a mosquito's stomach in Secunderabad on 20 August 1897. Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1902.

Infants and surprise: A. E. Stahl and L. Feigenson, 'Observing the unexpected enhances infants' learning and exploration', Science 348 (2015), 91 to 94. Eleven-month-olds explored and tested objects that had behaved surprisingly.
Meteorites: many scientists in Europe doubted that stones fall from the sky until E. F. F. Chladni (1794) and J.-B. Biot's report on the L'Aigle fall in France (1803).

Birds are living dinosaurs (theropods): accepted by most palaeontologists. The Himalayas are still rising by a few millimetres a year as the Indian plate pushes north. Octopuses have three hearts and copper-based blue blood.

Plato, Theaetetus 155d: wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder. Kena Upanishad 1.1: 'By whom willed does the mind go out?' The Upanishad takes its name from its first word, 'kena', meaning 'by whom'. Rig Veda 10.129.7, the end of the Nasadiya Sukta.

roots.context: We have tested haldi in our kitchen and heard about curious people from India and the world. Now we ask what being curious tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your haldi turned red where soap touched it, and stayed yellow with lemon, salt and sugar. Many people see haldi stains turn red in the wash. Seeing it does not tell you what made it red. Asking and testing told you, so discoveries can wait unnoticed in things everyone sees.
deep_truth.habit: We think discoveries are hidden far away, found only by special people in laboratories. But haldi stains have been turning red in washing buckets for a very long time. What was missing was someone asking why and trying one thing at a time.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Haldi Test, the child guessed first, then put six kitchen liquids on haldi paper, one in each box. Only soap and cooking soda turned it red. In the story, Paati had seen it for sixty years, and found out what did it only when Meenakshi asked and tested.

three.who_am_i: You are a curious being. Questions pop into your head without you trying, and you can test them.
three.what_is_life: Every living being explores. A baby tests a surprising toy, a crow pokes at something new, and a plant's roots search the soil for water.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of things nobody has asked about yet. Even your kitchen holds answers waiting for a question.

roots.thread: Questions are not only in people. A plant's roots search the soil, a crow turns over a new thing, an ant tries a new path. Everything is conscious in its own way, and every living being asks the world something and waits for an answer. When you asked the haldi a question with soap, the haldi answered in red. Being curious is one way the whole world comes to know itself.

teachings.teaching: Socrates, a thinker in ancient Greece, said that wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, a lover of wisdom. Wisdom has no other beginning than wonder.
teachings.link: Your haldi test began with wonder: why did the stain go red? The wondering came first, and the test came next.

teachings.teaching: This old Indian teaching begins with a question: 'By whom is the mind sent out?' It is even named after its first word, 'kena', which means 'by whom'. Asking is where it starts.
teachings.link: The Kena Upanishad starts with a question, the way a scientist does. You started with a question too, and the question led you to the answer.

teachings.teaching: This very old hymn asks how the world began. It ends by saying that perhaps even the highest one does not know. It is honest about not knowing.
teachings.link: Scientists also say 'we don't know yet' when they don't. Not knowing is where every new question, and every discovery, begins.

science.text: Even babies are curious. In one study, babies of about one year old tested toys that had done something surprising. They dropped or banged them to find out more.
Many animals explore new things, including crows, rats and octopuses. Scientists are still finding out how curiosity works in each of them.

other_view.view: Many scientists say only animals with brains can be curious. They say a plant's roots growing towards water follow a rule built into their cells, and that this is not the same as wondering.

practice.title: One minute of wonder
practice.say: Pick up one thing near you, like a leaf, a spoon or a grain of rice. Hold it in your hand. Look at it quietly for one whole minute. Turn it over. Feel it. Smell it. Now close your eyes and take one slow breath. Open them. Tell me one thing you wonder about it.
practice.kid: Pick up one small thing. Look at it for one minute. Feel it and smell it. Close your eyes and breathe. Now say one thing you wonder.

ask: Where do your questions come from?
Is there anything nobody will ever be able to find out?
When you asked the haldi a question with soap, did the haldi answer you?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged holding a single curry leaf close to her eyes, with a soft question mark of light above her and a kitchen window behind.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find a medicine for malaria? This card tells the true story of a scientist who found a clue in a very old book.
how_we_found_out.story: Malaria is an illness that people get from mosquito bites. In 1969, Tu Youyou, a scientist in Beijing, China, was asked to find a new medicine for it. The old medicines were no longer working well. Tu and her team read very old books of Chinese medicine. They tested hundreds of old recipes made from plants. Most did not work. One plant, sweet wormwood, sometimes worked and sometimes did not. Tu read the plant's recipe again, in a book written about 1,600 years ago by a doctor called Ge Hong. It said to soak the leaves in water, squeeze out the juice and drink all the juice. The book did not say to boil the leaves. Most plant medicines were made by boiling. Tu wondered if the heat was spoiling the medicine. She made it a new way, without much heat. In 1971 it worked on mice and monkeys. Then she and two people on her team took it themselves first, to check it was safe. The medicine, artemisinin, has since saved millions of lives. In 2015, Tu Youyou won the Nobel Prize, though she never had a doctorate.
how_we_found_out.who: Tu Youyou, a scientist in China, and her team, using a clue from Ge Hong, a doctor in China about 1,600 years ago
how_we_found_out.when: 1969 (Tu begins the search), 1971 (the low-heat medicine works in mice and monkeys), 1972 (first tests in people), 2015 (the Nobel Prize)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most people made plant medicines by boiling them, so boiled extracts of sweet wormwood were tried first, and they worked only sometimes. Tu guessed the heat was spoiling the medicine. Her low-heat extract worked every time in her tests, which showed the heat had been the problem.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist in a 1970s laboratory in Beijing, with a very old book open beside glass jars of green plant juice.
